vaclav-havel: Havel was born in Prague on 5 October 1936 into a wealthy family known in Czechoslovakia for its entrepreneurial and cultural achievements. His grandfather Vácslav Havel built an entertainment complex on Wenceslas Square, and his father, Václav Maria Havel, developed the Barrandov Terraces, beside which his uncle Miloš Havel built one of the largest film studios in Europe. Because of his bourgeois background his educational opportunities were limited under the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic. In the early 1950s he began a four-year apprenticeship as a chemical laboratory assistant while taking evening classes at a gymnasium.

After military service from 1957 to 1959, Havel found work in Prague's theatre world, first as a stagehand and then at the Theatre on Balustrade. His first full-length play performed in public was The Garden Party in 1963. In works such as The Garden Party and The Memorandum he used an absurdist style to criticise the communist system.

After the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968 and the suppression of the Prague Spring he was banned from the theatre and became more politically active. He worked at the Krakonoš brewery in Trutnov, an experience he drew on in his play Audience; it and two other plays featuring the character Ferdinand Vaněk circulated in samizdat. He helped found several dissident initiatives, including Charter 77, came under surveillance by the StB secret police and spent several periods as a political prisoner, the longest nearly four years, between 1979 and 1983.

His Civic Forum played a major role in the Velvet Revolution of 1989. On 29 December 1989 the Federal Assembly voted unanimously to make him President of Czechoslovakia. He had long insisted that change should come through autonomous civic initiatives rather than official institutions. He was re-elected in 1990 and again as the first president of the Czech Republic after Czechoslovakia dissolved on 31 December 1992.

Havel was instrumental in dismantling the Warsaw Pact and in the eastward enlargement of NATO. After leaving office in 2003 he remained a public intellectual, and from 1997 he hosted the annual conference Forum 2000. He died on 18 December 2011 at the age of 75 at his country home in Hrádeček. His political philosophy combined anti-consumerism, humanitarianism, environmentalism, civil activism and direct democracy. The international airport in Prague was renamed Václav Havel Airport Prague in 2012.
valencia: Valencia lies on the eastern coast of the Iberian Peninsula, fronting the Gulf of Valencia, on the highly fertile alluvial silts of the floodplain formed in the lower course of the Turia River. When the Romans founded it in 138 BCE it stood on the alluvial plain several kilometres from the sea. Its Latin name was Valentia, meaning strength or valour, and Livy says the colony was founded by Roman soldiers who had fought the Lusitanian rebel Viriatus.

Founded around 138 BCE as Valentia Edetanorum, Valencia is one of the oldest cities in Spain. It later became part of the Visigothic Kingdom and surrendered to the Moors around 714. In the wake of the fitna of al-Andalus it became the head of the independent Taifa of Valencia, which saw notable urban development. The Jewish poet and philosopher Solomon ibn Gabirol spent his last years there.

After Toledo fell in 1085 the territory became a protectorate of El Cid. A revolt in 1092 handed the city to the Almoravids, and in 1094 El Cid took it by force and established his own principality. With the Aragonese Christian conquest of 1238 Valencia became the capital of the Kingdom of Valencia. Its trade with the Iberian Peninsula and Italian ports made it thrive in the 15th century, and by the end of that century it had become one of the largest European cities. The University of Valencia was founded in 1499.

Between 1521 and 1522 the Revolt of the Brotherhoods plunged the kingdom into civil war, and Muslim vassals were forced to convert in 1526 at the behest of Charles V. Its economy suffered a crisis after the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609. The city became a major silk-manufacturing centre in the 18th century. During the Spanish Civil War it was the provisional seat of the Spanish Government from 1936 to 1937.

Valencia is the capital and largest city of the Valencian Community and of the province of the same name, and the third most populous city in Spain. Valencian and Spanish are the official languages. Its historic centre is among the largest in Spain, and its monuments include Valencia Cathedral, the Torres de Serrans, the Torres de Quart and the Lonja de la Seda, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996. The Falles festival, held in March, was recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage in 2016.
valladolid: Valladolid lies at about 735 metres above sea level in the centre of the Meseta Norte, where the Pisuerga and Esgueva rivers meet 15 km before they join the Duero. It is surrounded by winegrowing areas. The Vaccaei, a Celtic tribe, were the first people documented as a stable presence in this part of the middle Duero valley. The origin of the name is uncertain. One theory derives it from a Celtiberian expression meaning valley of waters, and another from the Arabic Balad al-Walid, city of al-Walid. In medieval texts the town is called Vallisoletum, sunny valley.

After the Muslim invasion of 711 the district stayed thinly settled until the Christians secured the whole Duero basin at the battle of Simancas in 939. In 1072 Alfonso VI of León and Castile gave the lordship of Valladolid to Count Pedro Ansúrez, who with his wife Eylo Alfónsez led the foundation of the town. The town grew rapidly in the 12th and 13th centuries, helped by commercial privileges from Alfonso VIII and Alfonso X, and the university dates from 1241. The earliest documented Jewish community dates to 1221.

Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon married in the city in 1469, and by the 15th century it was a residence of the kings of Castile. Christopher Columbus died there in 1506. In 1550 and 1551 the town held what is described as the first moral debate in European history on the treatment of indigenous peoples by conquerors. A fire in 1561 destroyed part of the city. Valladolid served briefly as the capital of the Hispanic Monarchy from 1601 to 1606 under the Duke of Lerma, valido of Philip III, before the court returned to Madrid.

Valladolid is the capital of the province of Valladolid and the seat of the government and parliament of the autonomous community of Castile and León, with a population of 299,816. Since the 1950s it has been an industrial centre, with an automotive industry that began with the founding of FASA-Renault in 1953. Its Holy Week processions and the Valladolid International Film Festival are held each year, and in 2019 it was recognised as a City of Film by UNESCO's Creative Cities Network.
valletta: Valletta lies between the Grand Harbour to the east and Marsamxett Harbour to the west, on the Sciberras peninsula. The peninsula's older names include Xagħret Mewwija, from the Arab period, and Sceberras, which recent scholarship derives from a Punic phrase meaning the headland or the middle peninsula. Before the city was built, the only structure on it was a small watchtower of 1488 dedicated to Saint Elmo.

The Order of Saint John had proposed building a city on the peninsula as early as 1524. In 1552 the watchtower was replaced by the larger Fort Saint Elmo, which fell to the Ottomans in the Great Siege of 1565 before the Order won the siege with Sicilian reinforcements. The victorious Grand Master Jean de Valette at once set out to build a fortified city that would bind the Knights to the island. Pope Pius V sent his military architect Francesco Laparelli to design it, and Philip II of Spain sent substantial money. De Valette laid the foundation stone on 28 March 1566, in what later became Our Lady of Victories Church. He died on 21 August 1568, aged 74, before the city was finished.

Laparelli laid the city out on a rectangular grid of wide, straight streets, a departure from the winding streets of medieval Maltese towns. After his death in 1570 the Maltese architect Girolamo Cassar oversaw the work. The city was mostly complete by the early 1570s, and it became the capital on 18 March 1571, when Grand Master Pierre de Monte moved from Fort St Angelo in Birgu to the Grandmaster's Palace. Seven auberges for the Order's Langues were finished by the 1580s. Under Grand Master Pinto, in the 18th century, many buildings were rebuilt in Baroque style.

The French invaded in 1798 and expelled the Order, and French troops held Valletta until they capitulated to the British in September 1800. Under British rule most of the fortifications were spared demolition and survive largely intact. The Malta Railway to Mdina opened in 1883 and closed in 1931. German and Italian air raids in the Second World War caused great destruction, including the loss of the Royal Opera House.

Valletta is the capital of Malta and one of its 68 council areas, with a population of 5,157 in 2021. It is Baroque in character, with 320 monuments in an area of 0.55 square kilometres, and is noted for its bastions, palaces, gardens and churches. The whole city has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980, and it was European Capital of Culture in 2018.
valparaiso: Valparaíso lies in central Chile, about 120 kilometres north-west of Santiago, on dozens of steep hillsides overlooking the Pacific Ocean. Its proximity to the Peru–Chile Trench, which stores large amounts of energy and sometimes ruptures in violent earthquakes, makes it vulnerable to them. The August 1906 earthquake devastated the city and killed nearly 3,000 people, and the 1730 Valparaíso earthquake and the 1985 Algarrobo earthquake were also significant. Residents are called porteños, Spanish for 'port dwellers'.

The first identifiable people of the bay were the Picunche, known for their agriculture. Spanish explorers arrived in 1536 aboard the Santiaguillo, a supply ship sent by Diego de Almagro for his expedition. Its commander, Juan de Saavedra, named the town after his native village of Valparaíso de Arriba in Cuenca Province, Spain; the town's original name was Alimapu or Quintil. Through the colonial period it remained a small village of a few houses and a church, attacked at times by English privateers, among them Francis Drake with the Golden Hind in 1578 and Richard Hawkins with the Dainty in 1594. Drake's sack of the town gave rise to the legend of the Cueva del Pirata.

The Chilean Navy has had its headquarters in the city since 1817. In the second half of the 19th century Valparaíso was a major stopover for ships travelling between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans by the Straits of Magellan, and in its golden age it drew many European immigrants and was known to sailors as Little San Francisco. It acquired Latin America's oldest stock exchange, the continent's first volunteer fire department, Chile's first public library and El Mercurio de Valparaíso, the oldest newspaper in the Spanish language in continuous publication. The opening of the Panama Canal in 1914 reduced ship traffic and dealt a serious blow to the port economy.

Valparaíso is the seat of the National Congress of Chile, which has met there since 1990, and the capital of the Valparaíso Region. Its historic quarter, a labyrinth of cobbled alleys and colourful buildings on the hills, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. Sixteen funiculars, called ascensores, remain, fifteen of them public and national monuments. The commune had 284,938 inhabitants at the 2024 census, within a Greater Valparaíso metropolitan area of 951,311.
vanuatu: Vanuatu is a Y-shaped archipelago of about 83 relatively small islands of volcanic origin, 65 of them inhabited, with about 1,300 kilometres between the most northern and southern islands. It lies 1,750 km east of northern Australia and 540 km northeast of New Caledonia. The largest island is Espiritu Santo, and the highest point is Mount Tabwemasana, at 1,879 metres. Most islands are steep, with unstable soils and little permanent freshwater. There are several active volcanoes, including Lopevi and Mount Yasur, and volcanic activity is common.

The history before European colonisation is mostly obscure, since no written sources predate contact and little archaeological work has been done. Evidence gathered since the 1980s supports the settlement of the islands about 3,000 years ago, between roughly 1100 BCE and 700 BCE, by people almost certainly of the Lapita culture. Notable Lapita sites include Teouma on Éfaté, which has a large ancient cemetery containing the remains of 94 individuals. Sites on Éfaté, Lelepa and Eretoka are associated with the 16th–17th century chief or chiefs called Roy Mata, a title possibly held by different men over several generations, who according to oral tradition united local clans and presided over an era of peace.

The first Europeans to visit were a Spanish expedition led by the Portuguese navigator Fernandes de Queirós, who reached Espíritu Santo in 1606 and claimed the archipelago for Spain as La Austrialia del Espíritu Santo. James Cook named it the New Hebrides in 1774, after the Hebrides of Scotland. In the 1880s France and the United Kingdom claimed parts of it, and in 1906 they agreed to manage it jointly as an Anglo-French condominium. An independence movement arose in the 1970s, and the Republic of Vanuatu was founded in 1980. The name combines vanua, meaning land or home, and tu, to stand; the first prime minister, Walter Lini, said it was meant to connote a country that has stood alone.

Vanuatu is a parliamentary democracy with a written constitution, and its capital is Port Vila on Efate. The official languages are Bislama, English and French, and Bislama, a creole with a mostly English-derived vocabulary, is the lingua franca. The Lapita sites became the country's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008. A national Council of Chiefs, the Malvatu Mauri, advises the government on culture and language, and chiefs remain leading figures at village level. The country is a member of the United Nations, the Commonwealth of Nations and the Pacific Islands Forum.
varanasi: Varanasi lies on the left, crescent-shaped bank of the Ganges, in the south-east of Uttar Pradesh, 121 kilometres downstream of Prayagraj. Traditional etymology links the name to two tributaries that bound the old city, the Varuna and the Assi. The city is known for its ghats, steps leading down the steep bank, where pilgrims perform rituals. At the Manikarnika and Harishchandra ghats Hindus cremate their dead, and the genealogy registers of Hindu families are kept in the city.

According to Hindu scriptures, Shiva founded Varanasi under its name Kashi. Excavations in 2014 found artefacts dating to 800 BCE, and digs nearby at Aktha and Ramnagar found objects from 1800 BCE. Kashi was a kingdom of the first millennium BCE, and the Buddha gave his first teaching at Sarnath. In the 8th century Adi Shankara established the worship of Shiva as an official sect of the city. In 1033 Ahmad Nialtagin, a subordinate of Mahmud of Ghazni, raided it and partly destroyed temples, but withdrew by midday because of the threat of local resistance.

Bhakti figures born there in the mid-second millennium include Kabir, Ravidas and Tulsidas, who wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi. Guru Nanak visited in 1507. The Benares Estate was established near the city in 1740, in the Mughal province of Awadh, and in 1775 the East India Company acquired Benares under the Treaty of Faizabad. It passed through the Ceded and Conquered Provinces in 1805, the North-Western Provinces in 1836 and the United Provinces in 1902, and became part of Uttar Pradesh in 1950.

The Kashi Vishwanath Temple and the Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple are among its notable shrines, and the Jantar Mantar observatory of 1737 stands above the ghats. Jonathan Duncan founded the Benares Sanskrit College in 1791, and Annie Besant and Madan Mohan Malviya founded the Banaras Hindu University in 1916. The city is a centre of silk weaving and carpets, and of music: the Benares gharana of tabla playing was developed there.
vasco-da-gama: Vasco da Gama was born in Sines, a seaport on the Alentejo coast of southwest Portugal. His father, Estêvão da Gama, had served as a knight of the household of Ferdinand, Duke of Viseu, rose in the ranks of the military Order of Santiago and was civil governor of Sines until 1478. Portuguese ships had worked down the African coast since the early 15th century, and Bartolomeu Dias had found the South Atlantic westerlies in 1487.

On 8 July 1497 da Gama left Lisbon with four ships and a crew of 170. After passing Sierra Leone he steered into the open ocean to catch the westerlies and made landfall on the African coast on 4 November 1497, having sailed more than 10,000 kilometres without touching land, the longest such journey made up to then. At Mozambique in March 1498 he posed as a Muslim to gain an audience with the sultan, but a hostile crowd drove him out. At Malindi a Gujarati pilot guided the fleet across the Indian Ocean.

The fleet anchored near Kozhikode on 20 May 1498. The Zamorin received da Gama, but the gifts were judged poor, Muslim merchants cast him as a pirate, and his request to leave a factor behind was turned down. The return crossing against the monsoon took more than 90 days, against 23 on the way out. Only about 55 men came home, and two ships were lost.

In 1502 da Gama commanded the fourth Portuguese India armada. Off Madayi he captured the pilgrim ship Mirim, which carried over 400 people, including about 50 women, and burned it with them aboard, according to the eyewitness Thomé Lopes and the chronicler Gaspar Correia. He then bombarded Kozhikode. Back in Portugal in September 1503, he was passed over when the first viceroy of India was named in 1505.

After Manuel I died in late 1521, King John III appointed da Gama governor of India, with the title of viceroy, in 1524. Da Gama contracted malaria soon after arriving and died in Cochin on 24 December 1524. His body was returned to Portugal in 1539. His voyage opened a sea route between Europe and India that the Portuguese held as a commercial monopoly for several decades. Luís de Camões wrote the national epic Os Lusíadas in his honour, while the killing of the pilgrims at sea has tempered his reputation.
vatican-city: The territory of Vatican City covers 44 hectares and forms part of the Vatican Hill and the adjacent former Vatican Fields, on the west bank of the Tiber. Until 1929 the area belonged to the Roman rione of Borgo. It is enclosed largely by walls: those of Leo IV (847–855), later expanded by fortifications built under Paul III (1534–1549), Pius IV (1559–1565) and Urban VIII (1623–1644).

St Peter's Square is set apart from Italian territory only by a white line along its limit. Some properties of the Holy See elsewhere in Rome and Italy, notably the Papal Palace of Castel Gandolfo and the major basilicas, have extraterritorial status similar to that of foreign embassies.

In the Roman Republic the name Vatican applied to the Ager Vaticanus, a marshy area on the west bank of the Tiber. Its closeness to the Etruscan city of Veii, an old enemy of Rome, and the floods of the Tiber led the Romans to regard it as dismal and ominous. Agrippina the Elder drained the area and laid out gardens there in the early 1st century CE, and in 40 CE her son, the emperor Caligula, built a circus for charioteers, later completed by Nero.

The Vatican obelisk in St Peter's Square is the last visible remnant of that circus. Caligula brought it from Heliopolis in Roman Egypt. The circus became a site of martyrdom for many Christians after the Great Fire of Rome in 64, and tradition states that Saint Peter was crucified upside-down there. In 1586 Pope Sixtus V moved the obelisk to its present position, using a method devised by the architect Domenico Fontana. The name Vatican City was first used in the Lateran Treaty, signed on 11 February 1929.

Vatican City is an absolute elective monarchy in which the pope holds legislative, executive and judicial power. Legislative authority is exercised in his name by the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State, a body of cardinals appointed for five-year periods. The state is distinct from the Holy See, which has existed as a juridical entity since Roman Imperial times and was not interrupted when it lacked territory between 1870 and 1929.

Citizenship rests on appointment to work in the service of the Holy See, not on birth, and usually ends when the appointment does. In 2024 the population was 882 residents, and a further 372 citizens lived elsewhere. Legislation uses only Italian. The state earns income from stamps, coins, museum admissions and publications, and uses the euro. UNESCO listed Vatican City as a World Heritage Site in 1984, the only site that consists of an entire state.
veliko-tarnovo: The old part of Veliko Tarnovo is built on three hills, Tsarevets, Trapezitsa and Sveta Gora, rising amid the meanders of the Yantra River. On Tsarevets stood the palaces of the Bulgarian emperors, the Patriarchate and the Patriarchal Cathedral, surrounded by thick walls. Trapezitsa is known for its many churches and as the former main residence of the nobility. The town has always held a strategic position on main roads connecting the western Balkans with the Black Sea and Eastern Europe with the Middle East. Its names Tarnovgrad and Tarnovo most probably come from the Old Bulgarian word for thorny, and the word veliko, meaning great, was added in 1965 in honour of its status as an old capital.

Veliko Tarnovo is one of the oldest settlements in Bulgaria, with a history of more than five millennia; the first traces of human presence, from the 3rd millennium BCE, were found on Trapezitsa. It was a stronghold of the First Bulgarian Empire, with an important military garrison. The Uprising of Asen and Peter began on 26 October 1185, the feast day of St. Demetrius of Thessaloniki, and ended with the restoration of Bulgaria as the Second Bulgarian Empire, ruled by the Asen dynasty, with Tarnovo as capital.

From the 12th to the 14th century Tarnovgrad was the strongest Bulgarian fortification and its most prosperous city, and the political, economic, cultural and religious centre of the empire. It covered about 70 hectares across the hills. The Bulgarian cleric Gregory Tsamblak described it in the 14th century as a very large, handsome city surrounded by walls, with 12,000 to 15,000 inhabitants. The Ottoman Empire captured it on 17 July 1393 after a three-month siege in which the Bulgarian Patriarch Evtimiy led the defence, and three years later conquered the entire Bulgarian Empire.

On 7 July 1877 the Russian general Joseph Vladimirovich Gourko liberated the city, ending 480 years of Ottoman rule. In 1878 the Treaty of Berlin created a Principality of Bulgaria between the Danube and the Stara Planina range, with its seat at Veliko Tarnovo. In the early 1950s, under Communist rule, the city underwent intensive urbanisation, expanding to the west.

Veliko Tarnovo is the administrative centre of Veliko Tarnovo Province in north central Bulgaria, often called the City of the Tsars. It had 68,783 inhabitants at the 2011 census. It is the seat of Veliko Tarnovo University, and its monuments include the Monument to the Asen Dynasty, built in 1985.
veneto: Veneto covers 18,398.9 square kilometres in the north-east of Italy. It is bordered by Friuli-Venezia Giulia to the east, Emilia-Romagna to the south, Lombardy to the west and Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol to the north, and in its northernmost corner it touches Austria. The climate is continental on the plains and milder along the Adriatic coast, around Lake Garda and in the hills. Rainfall is scarce near the river Po, about 750 millimetres a year, and much greater in the Prealps. The region is divided into seven provinces: Belluno, Padua, Rovigo, Treviso, Venice, Verona and Vicenza.

Between the 2nd and 1st millennium BCE the region was inhabited by the Euganei. Ancient historians derived the Veneti from Paphlagonia in Anatolia, led by Prince Antenor, a comrade of Aeneas, at the time of the fall of Troy, which may have been an attempt to link Venetic origins with the legend of Roman origins in Troy. Other historians link them with the Celts. In the 3rd century BCE the Veneti sided with Rome, and during the Second Punic War they sent soldiers against Hannibal, some of whom were killed at the Battle of Cannae in 216 BCE. The region remained part of the Roman Empire until the 5th century CE.

By the middle of the 8th century the Franks controlled the mainland, which became part of the Carolingian Empire. When invaders threatened the wealth of the mainland, part of the population took refuge on islands in the lagoon, where Venice arose. It became an independent maritime republic ruled by an elected doge, and it ruled the region until 1797. Napoleon's armies conquered Veneto in 1805–1806, and after the Congress of Vienna of 1814–1815 it formed the eastern half of the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia within the Austrian Empire. The region joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1866 after the Third Italian War of Independence and a plebiscite.

Veneto is one of the 20 regions of Italy, with 4,857,460 inhabitants. Venice is the capital and Verona the largest city. Most inhabitants speak Venetian as well as Italian. The regional Statute, first promulgated on 22 May 1971, speaks of the Venetian people, though the region does not have the special statute of its neighbours Friuli-Venezia Giulia and Trentino-Alto Adige. Under Austrian rule the agricultural economy suffered, and nearly 3 million Venetians left between 1861 and 1961, many for Brazil and Argentina. Millions of people of Venetian descent now live abroad, especially in southern Brazil, where places such as Nova Veneza and Nova Treviso recall their origin.
venice: Venice is built on an archipelago of more than a hundred islands in the shallow Venetian Lagoon, an enclosed bay of about 550 square kilometres between the mouths of the Po and the Piave. The islands are separated by canals and linked by several hundred bridges, and the historic centre is divided into six districts, or sestieri. Those who sought refuge on the islands of Torcello, Iesolo and Malamocco learned to drive closely spaced piles of alder trunks into the mud until they reached compressed clay, and laid plates of Istrian limestone on top. Subsidence contributes to the seasonal acqua alta, when the lowest surfaces are covered at high tide.

No surviving record deals directly with the founding of Venice. Tradition and the evidence have led several historians to agree that the first inhabitants were refugees from nearby Roman cities such as Padua, Aquileia, Treviso, Altinum and Concordia, and from the countryside, fleeing Germanic and Hun invasions. The traditional founding is the dedication of the church of San Giacomo on the islet of Rialto, said to have taken place at noon on 25 March 421. The city was the capital of the Republic of Venice from 810 to 1797, when Napoleon ended its sovereignty, and in 1866 it became part of the Kingdom of Italy.

Early prosperity probably owed much to the trade in slaves captured in central Europe and sold to North Africa and the Levant. The city later controlled a vast sea empire and was considered the first real international financial centre, reaching its fullest prominence in the 14th century. The Venetian Arsenal, the base of its naval power, is considered by several historians to be the first factory in history. Its population was 60,000 in 1000, 80,000 in 1200, between 110,000 and 180,000 in 1300, and approached 200,000 by 1600.

The municipality had 254,850 residents in 2021, of whom 50,434 lived in the historic island city. Within the historic centre transport remains entirely on water or on foot, and the gondola survives mainly for tourists and ceremonies. The lagoon and the city were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. Marco Polo and Giacomo Casanova were Venetian writers, and the composers Tomaso Albinoni and Antonio Vivaldi were born there.
verica: Verica's coinage presents him as a son of Commius and king of the Atrebates, a tribe that was probably Belgic. His predecessors are likely to have influenced a wide area covering Berkshire, Surrey, western Kent, Sussex, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. The distribution of his own coins shows a much smaller kingdom, limited to modern Sussex and east Hampshire, with its capital in or near the later Roman town of Noviomagus Reginorum, the modern Chichester. He succeeded his elder brother Eppillus in about 15 CE.

He may also have ruled the northern Atrebatic kingdom at Calleva Atrebatum, the modern Silchester. Rome recognised him as rex, and he appears to have had friendly trading and diplomatic links with the empire, perhaps in an attempt to restore the kingdom to its former strength. Unlike those of nearby areas, the hillforts in the core of his kingdom show no sign of refortification, which implies that its inhabitants were well disposed to Rome.

The Catuvellauni pressed on his territory from the east. Epaticcus, brother of Cunobelinus, conquered Calleva in about 25 CE. After the death of Epaticcus about 35 CE Verica regained some territory, but Caratacus, the son of Cunobelinus, conquered the entire kingdom some time after 40 CE. By the time of his expulsion the kingdom had been reduced to a core around Chichester and the Manhood Peninsula.

Dio Cassius records that a Berikos, widely taken to be Verica, fled to the emperor Claudius because of a revolt, and Suetonius mentions British demands that Rome return certain deserters. His ties with Rome have been used to argue that the invasion landed on the south coast and not at the traditional site of Richborough in Kent. He may have been restored afterwards, but this is not attested, and a new ruler of the region, Cogidubnus, soon appeared; he may have been Verica's heir.

Most scholars take Verica to have been a man. The archaeologist Miles Russell has argued that Verica was a woman, citing the ending of the name and the horsewomen on the coinage. Roger Tomlin disputes this, since no female client ruler is known to have used the title rex, and Daphne Nash notes that some coins show Verica with an Adam's apple and in male priestly dress.
victor-hugo: Victor-Marie Hugo was born on 26 February 1802 in Besançon, the youngest son of Joseph Léopold Sigisbert Hugo, a general in the Napoleonic army, and Sophie Trébuchet. His father was an atheist and an ardent supporter of the Republic, while his mother was loyal to the deposed dynasty. Because his father was an officer, the family moved often from posting to posting. In 1810 his father was made Count Hugo de Cogolludo y Sigüenza by Joseph Bonaparte, then King of Spain, though the Spanish title seems not to have been legally recognised in France.

In his youth Hugo resolved to be Chateaubriand or nothing, and his life came to parallel that of the older writer in many ways. Like him, he furthered the cause of Romanticism, became involved in politics and was forced into exile. He married Adèle Foucher in October 1822.

Hugo published his first novel, Hans of Iceland, in 1823 and his second, Bug-Jargal, in 1826. His five volumes of poetry between 1829 and 1840 cemented his reputation as one of the great elegiac and lyric poets of his time. The Hunchback of Notre-Dame appeared in 1831 and Les Misérables in 1862. He was at the forefront of Romanticism with his play Cromwell and his drama Hernani. After three unsuccessful attempts he was elected to the Académie française in 1841, and he wrote the libretto of Louise Bertin's opera La Esmeralda in 1836.

Politically he moved from royalism toward republicanism. Louis Philippe I appointed him a peer of France in 1845, where he spoke against the death penalty and social injustice and for freedom of the press. Elected in 1848 to the National Assembly of the Second Republic as a conservative, he broke with the conservatives in 1849 with a speech calling for an end to misery and poverty. His campaign to abolish the death penalty was known internationally.

When Louis Napoleon seized complete power in 1851, Hugo openly declared him a traitor to France. He moved to Brussels, then to Jersey, from which he was expelled for supporting the newspaper L'Homme. He settled at Hauteville House in Saint Peter Port, Guernsey, in self-imposed exile from October 1855 until 1870. He returned to Paris in 1870 and was hailed as a national hero. He lost a bid for re-election to the National Assembly in 1872 and was elected to the new Senate on 30 January 1876.

Hugo died on 22 May 1885, aged 83. He was given a state funeral in the Panthéon of Paris, attended by over two million people, the largest in French history. He produced more than 4,000 drawings, with about 3,000 surviving. His portrait was placed on French currency.
vienna: Vienna lies in north-eastern Austria at the easternmost extension of the Alps, on the eastern edge of the Vienna Woods and at the transition to the Pannonian Basin. The earliest settlement, on the site of the inner city, lay south of the meandering Danube, and the city now spans both banks. It is both a city and one of the nine states of Austria. The name is a Latinised form of the German Wien, which comes from the River Wien and first appears in the Salzburg Annals, recording a battle at a place called Wenia in 881.

In the 1st century the Romans set up the military camp of Vindobona, in the province of Pannonia, near the Danube to secure the frontier. Construction of the legionary camp began around 97 CE, and the settlement at its peak had about 15,000 people. The emperor Marcus Aurelius may have died here in 180. The city was rebuilt after a Germanic invasion and served as a seat of Roman government until the fifth century, when its people fled the Huns and the site was abandoned for several centuries.

In 1155 Vienna became the seat of the Babenbergs, who ruled Austria from 976 to 1246, and in 1221 it was granted city rights. In the 16th century the Habsburgs made it the seat of the emperors of the Holy Roman Empire, which it remained until the empire's dissolution in 1806, with only a brief interruption. With the formation of the Austrian Empire in 1804 it became the capital of that empire and of all its successor states.

As capital of Austria-Hungary from 1867 to 1918 it grew sharply, and in 1910 it had more than two million inhabitants and was the third-largest city in Europe after London and Paris. Under the Nazi regime 65,000 Jews were deported from Vienna and murdered, and about 130,000 fled.

Vienna is the capital and most populous city of Austria, with just over two million inhabitants. The historic centre was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001 and includes Baroque palaces and gardens and the Ringstrasse of the late 19th century. Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart, Schubert and Brahms were among the composers who worked there, and Sigmund Freud, the first psychoanalyst, lived there too. Since 1980 the city has been a United Nations headquarters city.
vietnam: Vietnam lies on the eastern Indochinese Peninsula, with a total area of about 331,000 square kilometres, a coastline 3,444 kilometres long and land boundaries of 4,639 kilometres. At its narrowest point, in Quảng Trị province, it is as little as 50 kilometres across, and in the north it widens to around 600 kilometres.

The land is mostly hilly and densely forested, with level land covering no more than 20%. The Red River flows past Hanoi into the Gulf of Tonkin, and its delta, a plain of 15,000 square kilometres, has the highest population density of any region; its sediment advances the delta 60 to 80 metres into the South China Sea every year.

Humans lived in what is now Vietnam as early as the Paleolithic, and Homo erectus fossils dating to around 500,000 BCE have been found in caves in the north. By about 1,000 BCE wet-rice cultivation in the Ma River and Red River floodplains led to the Đông Sơn culture, known for its bronze casting and elaborate bronze drums.

Vietnamese legends hold that the Hồng Bàng dynasty of the Hùng kings, first established in 2879 BCE, was the first state, known as Văn Lang. In 257 BCE the last Hùng king was defeated by Thục Phán, who formed Âu Lạc and proclaimed himself An Dương Vương. The Han dynasty annexed northern and central Vietnam, which were then under Chinese rule from 111 BCE until the first dynasty emerged in 939.

Successive monarchical dynasties absorbed Chinese influences through Confucianism and Buddhism and expanded southward to the Mekong Delta, conquering Champa. During most of the 17th and 18th centuries Vietnam was effectively divided into two domains, Đàng Trong and Đàng Ngoài. The Nguyễn, the last imperial dynasty, surrendered to France in 1883, and in 1887 the territory was integrated into French Indochina as three separate regions. The Viet Minh launched the August Revolution and declared independence in 1945. France returned and was defeated in the First Indochina War in 1954, after which Vietnam was divided into two parts.

The Vietnam War was fought between communist North Vietnam, supported by the Soviet Union and China, and anti-communist South Vietnam, supported by the United States. After the North Vietnamese victory in 1975 the country reunified as a communist state under the Communist Party of Vietnam. An ineffective planned economy, a Western trade embargo and wars with Cambodia and China crippled it further, and in 1986 the party launched the Đổi Mới reforms toward a socialist-oriented market economy. Vietnam joined the World Trade Organization in 2007. Its population was 96,208,984 in the 2019 census; the Kinh make up 85.32% of it, and 54 ethnic groups are officially recognised.
vietnam-war: Vietnam had been under French control as part of French Indochina since the 1880s. After the French defeat in the First Indochina War, Vietnam's independence was affirmed at the 1954 Geneva Conference, which divided the country at the 17th parallel. The communists under Ho Chi Minh took power in North Vietnam, while an anticommunist regime under Ngô Đình Diệm took control of South Vietnam with United States backing. The North Vietnamese supplied and eventually directed the Viet Cong, a communist front in the south that intensified a guerrilla war from 1957. The war was at once a postcolonial war of national liberation, a theatre of the Cold War and a civil war. In 1963 Diệm was killed in a US-backed military coup.

After the Gulf of Tonkin incident of August 1964, the US Congress passed a resolution that gave President Lyndon B. Johnson authority to increase the military presence without declaring war. On 8 March 1965, 3,500 US Marines landed near Da Nang, the start of the ground war, and deployment rose to 536,000 by 1969. The Tet Offensive of 1968 was a tactical defeat for the communists but contributed to growing American opposition to the war. Richard Nixon began Vietnamization from 1969, in which an expanded South Vietnamese army took over the fighting as US forces withdrew. Fighting spilled into Laos and Cambodia.

After the Paris Peace Accords of 1973 the last American forces left, but fighting continued. In March 1975 North Vietnamese forces opened an offensive in the Central Highlands, and the South Vietnamese army collapsed. Saigon fell on 30 April 1975, after the largest helicopter evacuation in history, Operation Frequent Wind.

North and South Vietnam were merged in July 1976 as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. Estimates of the dead vary widely. About 58,220 US service members died, and estimates run from 275,000 to 310,000 Cambodians and 20,000 to 62,000 Laotians. The war was marked by atrocities, among them the massacres at Huế and Mỹ Lai, and some 20 percent of South Vietnam's jungle was sprayed with toxic herbicides, which led to significant health problems. Political repression and flawed economic policies after the war precipitated the flight of the Vietnamese boat people, of whom about 250,000 perished at sea. In the United States the war gave rise to Vietnam syndrome, an aversion to overseas military involvement.
vikings: The Viking Age is taken to run from the earliest recorded raid by Norsemen in 793 to the Norman conquest of England in 1066. In England it began on 8 June 793, when Norsemen destroyed the abbey on the island of Lindisfarne. The Northumbrian scholar Alcuin of York declared that never before had such an atrocity been seen, and medieval Christians could find no explanation for the suffering save the wrath of God.

The Vikings raided, traded, acted as mercenaries and settled over a wide area. Early raiders probably returned home, but later Vikings settled in the British Isles, the Faroe Islands, Iceland, Greenland, Normandy and the Baltic coast, and along the Dnieper and Volga routes, where they were known as Varangians. Vikings under Leif Erikson reached North America and set up short-lived settlements at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland. Two Vikings ruled England: Sweyn Forkbeard claimed the throne from 1013 to 1014, and his son Cnut the Great was king from 1016 to 1035. By the late 11th century the Church was legitimising royal dynasties, and the three kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden were taking shape.

Viking society was divided into thralls, karls and jarls, a structure described in the Eddic poem Rígsþula and confirmed by archaeology. Most Vikings were farmers, fishermen, craftsmen and traders. They spoke Old Norse and wrote inscriptions in runes, usually short and formulaic, so most contemporary written sources come from Christian and Islamic communities outside Scandinavia, often by authors who had suffered from Viking activity. They followed the Old Norse religion for most of the period and became Christians over the 8th to 12th centuries.

Their longships had a long, narrow hull and shallow draught, with oars to complement the sail, which let crews land in shallow water. Scandinavia used little coinage outside trading centres such as Ribe and Hedeby, so exchange rested on the weight and purity of silver, measured with small portable scales.

The Vikings influenced Old English, and so Modern English. The Normans descended from Vikings given overlordship of the Duchy of Normandy in the 10th century. Not until the 1890s did scholars outside Scandinavia begin to reassess Viking artistry, technology and seamanship. There is no evidence that Viking warriors wore horned helmets, a costume element that first appeared in the 19th century.
vikramaditya-i: Vikramaditya was one of several sons of Pulakeshin II; the later Chalukyas of Kalyani made him a son of Pulakeshin's son Adityavarman, a statement that can be dismissed as inaccurate. Pulakeshin was defeated and probably killed when the Pallavas invaded Vatapi around 642, and the history of the next decade is unclear. The throne may have passed to Adityavarman, his son Abhinavaditya and then another brother, Chandraditya, whose widow Vijaya-Bhattarika appears to have acted as regent for their minor son.

During that regency Vikramaditya seems to have risen as supreme commander of the army and ruler in practice. His inscriptions say that he recovered the regal fortune of his father, which had been concealed by three kings. The historian K. A. Nilakanta Sastri took these to include his brothers and supposed a partition of the kingdom, but there is no evidence of one; D. C. Sircar and others hold that he fought the Pallavas as a subordinate of his brothers and took the throne only after their deaths. His Gadval inscription of about 674, dated to his twelfth regnal year, places his accession about 655.

With the help of his maternal grandfather, a king of the Western Ganga dynasty, Vikramaditya ended a Pallava occupation that had lasted thirteen years. He gave his loyal younger brother Jayasimhavarma the viceroyalty of Lata in southern Gujarat. Against the Pallava kings Mahendravarman II and Paramesvaravarman I he allied himself with the Pandyas, and by 670 he had a military camp at Malliyur, west of Kanchipuram. Chalukya records claim that he defeated Paramesvaravarman I and took Kanchi but did not destroy it; the writer Anirudh Kanisetti holds that the city was sacked.

Chalukya records place him in camp at Uragapura on the south bank of the Kaveri river on 25 April 674. At Peruvalanallur he met Paramesvaravarman I and a Pandya king, and Pallava and Pandya records alike claim that the Chalukyas were defeated there. Pallava inscriptions also speak of the destruction of the city of Ranarasika, an epithet of Vikramaditya, but several historians question whether Vatapi was sacked a second time; Chalukya records credit his son Vinayaditya and grandson Vijayaditya with defeating the invaders.

Vikramaditya bore titles that advertised his military power, among them Rana-rasika, lover of war, Anivarita, unopposed, and Raja-malla, royal wrestler. He was married to the Western Ganga princess Gangamahadevi. Under him the Chalukya kingdom recovered most of the territory it had controlled under Pulakeshin II. He died in 680 and was succeeded by his son Vinayaditya.
vilnius: Vilnius lies at the confluence of the Vilnia and Neris rivers in southeastern Lithuania, 312 km from the Baltic Sea and the main Lithuanian seaport, Klaipėda. The city covers 402 km2, of which 68.8 per cent is green space. Its name comes from the river Vilnia, an old Lithuanian name meaning ripple, which was transferred to the city. The name first appears in Latin letters of Grand Duke Gediminas in 1323, in the form Vilna, and in 1325 as Wilno, a form still used in Polish. The Lithuanian form Vilnius was recorded around 1600 in the Postil of Mikalojus Daukša and became widespread during the national revival at the end of the 19th century.

The history of Vilnius goes back to the Stone Age. From at least 1323 until 1795 the city was the capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and from the 13th century until the mid-17th century the Vilnius Castle Complex was the residence of the Lithuanian monarchs. Magdeburg rights were granted in 1378, and a magistrate or city council, subordinate to the ruler, then governed it.

In 1517 the Italian princess Bona Sforza married the Lithuanian Grand Duke Sigismund I the Old, which strengthened the Italian influence on the city's Renaissance and Baroque architecture. Vilnius became an artistic centre of the Grand Duchy, attracting artists from across Europe. Under the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth it was noted for its multicultural population, which contemporary sources compared to Babylon. Before World War II and the Holocaust it was one of Europe's most important Jewish centres.

Later Vilnius was ruled by imperial and Soviet Russia, Napoleonic France, Imperial and Nazi Germany and interwar Poland, and it again became a capital of Lithuania in the 20th century. Before World War II Poles made up the majority of inhabitants, and the population exchange between Poland and Soviet Lithuania after the war changed that.

Vilnius is the capital and largest city of Lithuania and the most populous city in the Baltic states. Its Old Town, considered one of the largest and best-preserved in Europe, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994. The Baroque style known as Vilnian Baroque is named after the city, which is the easternmost Baroque city and the largest north of the Alps. Around two thirds of its residents were Lithuanians in 2021.
vincent-van-gogh: Vincent Willem van Gogh was born on 30 March 1853 in Groot-Zundert, in the predominantly Catholic province of North Brabant. He was the oldest surviving child of Theodorus van Gogh, a minister of the Dutch Reformed Church, and Anna Cornelia Carbentus. His grandfather, also named Vincent, was a prominent art dealer, and three of that grandfather's six sons became art dealers. His younger brother Theo was born on 1 May 1857. Van Gogh was taught at home, then sent to boarding school at Zevenbergen and in 1866 to the middle school in Tilburg, where he was deeply unhappy. He returned home in March 1868 and later wrote that his youth was "austere and cold, and sterile."

As an adult he began painting at an elementary level. In early 1882 his uncle Cornelis Marinus, owner of a gallery in Amsterdam, commissioned drawings of The Hague but was twice disappointed. Theo gave him money for materials in August 1882. From early 1883 Van Gogh worked on multi-figure compositions, and he destroyed several large paintings made at Nuenen; The Potato Eaters and its companion pieces are the only ones to survive. In November 1885 he travelled to Antwerp and later to Paris, where he met Émile Bernard and Paul Gauguin. His colours grew brighter, and his style was fully realised during his stay in Arles in 1888, when he painted series of olive trees, wheat fields and sunflowers.

The correspondence with Theo is the most comprehensive primary source on his work. It includes more than 600 letters from Vincent to Theo, and most of what is known of his theories of art is recorded in them.

Van Gogh suffered from psychotic episodes and delusions. His friendship with Gauguin ended after a confrontation with a razor, when he severed part of his own left ear. He spent time in psychiatric hospitals, including one at Saint-Rémy, and then moved to the Auberge Ravoux in Auvers-sur-Oise, where he came under the care of Dr Paul Gachet. On 27 July 1890 he shot himself in the chest and died two days later.

His reputation grew steadily among artists and critics after exhibitions in the late 1880s. Theo died in January 1891, and Theo's widow Jo van Gogh-Bonger took charge of the paintings and letters. Memorial exhibitions were held in several cities, and in 1896 the young Henri Matisse was introduced to Van Gogh's work and turned to bright colours. The Fauves and German Expressionists later took up elements of his style.
virgil: Biographical information about Virgil comes chiefly from ancient vitae, or lives, prefixed to commentaries on his work by Probus, Donatus and Servius. The life given by Donatus is thought to reproduce closely a lost life by Suetonius. Some of this evidence relies on allegory and on inferences drawn from his poetry, so details of his life are considered somewhat problematic.

According to the vitae, Publius Vergilius Maro was born on 15 October 70 BCE in the village of Andes, near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul, in what is now northern Italy. His ancestry is uncertain, and scholars have proposed Etruscan, Celtic, Venetic, Ligurian or Greek origins. Most sources say his father was an employee of an apparitor named Magius, whose daughter he married. Phocas and Probus give his mother's name as Magia Polla. Confusion between the family name Magius and the noun magus, 'magician', probably contributed to the medieval legend that Virgil was a magician.

The commentators say Virgil began school at five and later went to Cremona, Milan and finally Rome to study rhetoric, medicine and astronomy, which he abandoned for philosophy. His admiring references to Asinius Pollio and Cinna have led scholars to infer that he was for a time associated with the neoteric circle of Catullus. According to the Catalepton, he began to write poetry while in the Epicurean school of Siro in Naples. A group of small works attributed to him by the commentators, the Appendix Vergiliana, is considered spurious by modern scholars, with the possible exception of some short pieces.

The Eclogues are ten poems in dactylic hexameter, roughly modelled on the pastoral poetry of the Hellenistic poet Theocritus. Eclogues 1 and 9 address the land confiscations and their effects on the Italian countryside. Eclogue 4, addressed to Asinius Pollio and called the Messianic Eclogue, uses the imagery of a golden age in connection with the birth of a child whose identity has been debated. Virgil is credited with establishing Arcadia as a poetic ideal. Modern scholars largely reject attempts to draw his biography from the characters of the poems.

His works revolutionised Latin poetry almost from publication, and the Eclogues, Georgics and above all the Aeneid became standard school texts. Ovid parodied the opening of the Aeneid, Lucan wrote an anti-Virgilian epic, and Statius and Silius Italicus engaged closely with him. Servius, a commentator of the 4th century CE, based his work on that of Donatus. Augustine of Hippo confessed that he had wept at reading the death of Dido. In the Divine Comedy Dante presents Virgil as his guide through Hell and most of Purgatory.
virginia: Virginia, officially the Commonwealth of Virginia, lies between the Atlantic coast and the Appalachian Mountains and borders Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, West Virginia and Maryland. Central Virginia lies mostly in the Piedmont, the foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains, and the Shenandoah Valley holds the state's most productive farmland. Hampton Roads is the site of the region's main seaport and of Naval Station Norfolk.

Hunter-gatherers are estimated to have reached Virginia about 17,000 years ago, and Daugherty's Cave was in regular use as a rock shelter by 9,800 years ago. Farming spread in the late Woodland period, between 500 and 1000 CE. In the 1500s the native population within the present boundaries reached about 50,000. From the 1570s some thirty tribes of Tsenacommacah consolidated under Wahunsenacawh, commonly called Chief Powhatan, forming the Powhatan Confederacy, which governed more than 150 settlements with about 15,000 people in 1607. Three-quarters of the native population died of smallpox and other Old World diseases during that century.

In 1607 the London Company founded the Colony of Virginia, the first permanent English colony in the New World, which gave the state its nickname of the Old Dominion. Enslaved people from Africa and land taken from displaced native peoples fed the plantation economy and also fuelled conflict. The first General Assembly met in July 1619 and is the oldest lawmaking body in North America. Virginians fought in the American Revolution. In the American Civil War the state government in Richmond joined the Confederacy, while many north-western counties stayed loyal to the Union, which led to the separation of West Virginia in 1863.

The capital is Richmond and the most populous city is Virginia Beach; more than a third of the state's people live in Northern Virginia. The 2020 census counted 8,631,393 residents. The state's motto is Sic Semper Tyrannis, Thus Always to Tyrants. Eight Virginians have been President of the United States, including four of the first five, which gave it the name Mother of Presidents. It is governed under its seventh constitution, approved in 1970.
vishnu: Vishnu is a Rigvedic solar deity, but he does not figure prominently in the Rigveda compared with Indra and Agni: only five of its 1,028 hymns are dedicated to him. Some scholars, among them F. B. J. Kuiper and Jan Gonda, argue that he must have been a more important figure than his infrequent appearances suggest. He rose to prominence in the Brahmana layer of the Vedas in the mid-first millennium BCE. In the last centuries BCE and the early centuries CE he was identified with local traditions and deities, particularly the Bhagavata deities Vasudeva-Krishna and Gopala-Krishna and the Pancharatra deity Narayana, and became a divinity of the highest rank, equivalent to the Supreme Being.

Vishnu is the Supreme Being within Vaishnavism and the preserver in the Trimurti, the triad that includes Brahma and Shiva. His name means all pervasive. In Vaishnava belief he creates, protects and transforms the universe, and he is depicted sleeping on the coils of the serpent Shesha in the primeval ocean of milk with his consort Lakshmi. Whenever the world is threatened with evil he descends as an avatar to restore the cosmic order and protect dharma. The Dashavatara are the ten primary avatars, of which Rama and Krishna are the most worshipped.

In iconography he has dark blue, blue-grey or black skin and is usually shown with four arms, wearing jewels. When he descends as Rama and Krishna, Lakshmi appears as Sita and Radha or Rukmini. His mount is the eagle Garuda.

Vishnu is the main subject of the Vaishnava Puranas, of which the most important are the Bhagavata Purana, Vishnu Purana, Nāradeya Purana, Garuda Purana and Vayu Purana. The Tamil Sangam literature, mostly from the early centuries CE, reveres him as Mayon, the dark one. Ideas about Vishnu became important to the Bhakti movement, which swept India after the 12th century. The Alvars, Tamil Vaishnava poet-saints, sang his praises as they travelled and established temple sites such as Srirangam, and their poems were compiled as the Divya Prabhandham.
vladimir-lenin: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov was born in Simbirsk on 22 April 1870 (10 April O.S.), the third of eight children. His father, Ilya Nikolayevich Ulyanov, came from a family of former serfs and rose to be Director of Public Schools for the province, a post that carried hereditary nobility. Lenin took up revolutionary socialist politics after his brother's execution in 1887 and was expelled from Kazan Imperial University for protesting against the Tsarist government. In late 1893 he moved to Saint Petersburg and rose to a senior position in a Marxist cell. Arrested for sedition in 1897, he argued in prison that industrial capitalism had created a proletariat that would overthrow Tsarism. He was exiled to Siberia, where he married Nadezhda Krupskaya.

In 1903 Lenin took a key part in the split of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party and led the Bolshevik faction. After the failed Revolution of 1905 he campaigned for the First World War to be turned into a Europe-wide proletarian revolution. He returned to Russia after the February Revolution of 1917 and helped lead the October Revolution, in which the Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government.

His government at first shared power with the Left Socialist Revolutionaries. The Constituent Assembly elected in November 1917 gave the Bolsheviks about a quarter of the vote; it met in January 1918 and was forcibly disbanded. By 1919 Mensheviks and Socialist Revolutionaries had been expelled from the soviets and Russia was a one-party state. The government redistributed land, nationalised banks and large industry, left the First World War by a treaty conceding territory, and won the Russian Civil War. Opponents were suppressed in the Red Terror, in which tens of thousands were killed or interned. In 1921 Lenin encouraged economic growth through the New Economic Policy.

Lenin fell seriously ill in 1921, suffered strokes in May and December 1922, and died at Gorki on 21 January 1924. Joseph Stalin succeeded him as the pre-eminent figure in the Soviet government. His interpretation of Marxism, first called Leninism by Martov in 1904, became the basis of Marxism-Leninism and a model for later Communist-led states. Supporters see him as a champion of revolutionary socialism and internationalism, while critics accuse him of establishing a totalitarian dictatorship that carried out mass killings and political repression.
vladivostok: Vladivostok stands around the Golden Horn Bay on the southern extremity of the Muravyov-Amursky Peninsula, about 45 kilometres from the border between China and Russia and 134 kilometres from the border with North Korea. Its name means Lord of the East or Ruler of the East, from the Slavic word for to rule and the Russian word for east. The area was historically part of Outer Manchuria. Some modern Chinese historians claim a Chinese settlement stood on the site around 600 CE under the name Yongmingcheng.

Russia gained the territory from Qing China under the Treaty of Aigun, confirmed by the Convention of Peking, and the city was founded as a military outpost on 2 July 1860. The first civilian settler, the merchant Yakov Lazarevich Semyonov, arrived in 1861. In the early 1870s the main naval base of the Siberian Military Flotilla was moved there from Nikolaevsk-on-Amur, which set off a construction boom. The first urban plan, by Mikhail Lubensky, dates from 1868, and the railway station was completed in 1894. The Trans-Siberian Railway, finished in 1905, linked Moscow with Vladivostok, Russia's most important Pacific port.

From the late 1890s to the early 1920s half of the population was Asian, the Chinese being the largest group, followed by Koreans and Japanese. The Chinese quarter, called Millionka, held up to 50,000 people at its peak. Koreans moved to the area in large numbers after Japan annexed Korea in 1910, and by 1915 about 10,000 lived in the city. Their enclave, Sinhanch'on, became a hub of the Korean independence movement and hosted the first Korean provisional government, the Korean Independence Army Government. On the orders of Joseph Stalin both quarters were liquidated and their residents deported between 1936 and 1938.

After the Russian Revolution of 1917, White Russian and Allied forces occupied Vladivostok in 1918. The last of them, from Japan, were not withdrawn until 1922, and the Red Army took the city the same year. By then it was in decline, and its population had fallen to 106,000. Under the New Economic Policy of 1923 to 1925 the commercial port reopened and became the most profitable in the country.

Vladivostok is the administrative centre of Primorsky Krai and the largest Russian port on the Pacific Ocean. It is the home of the headquarters of the Pacific Fleet of the Russian Navy and the starting point of the Trans-Siberian portion of the Eurasian Land Bridge. Its population passed 500,000 in the 1970s and reached a high of over 648,000 in 1992. More than 90 per cent of residents declare Russian ethnicity, though minorities of Koreans and Chinese remain.
vlore: Vlorë lies on the Bay of Vlorë in south-western Albania, on the eastern side of the Strait of Otranto, surrounded by the foothills of the Ceraunian Mountains. The bay forms a natural harbour, which gave the site a significant place in antiquity as a base for trade. The name comes from the ancient Greek Aulon, meaning channel or glen, first recorded in the 2nd century CE by Lucian and Ptolemy. The Albanian form Vlorë developed by a sound change, rhotacism, from Vlonë, while the Italian Valona and the Turkish Avlonya come from the Greek name.

The coast of Vlorë was among the Illyrian sites with pre-urban activity from the 11th to 10th centuries BCE, and Greek colonists are traditionally believed to have founded Orikos, Thronion and Aulon on these shores. A large fortified port town, inhabited from the 6th century BCE to the 2nd century CE, lies partly submerged at Triport to the north-west; it may have been moved to the site of the modern city. Aulon was an important port of the Roman Empire, in the province of Epirus Nova, and became an episcopal see in the 5th century.

In the 11th and 12th centuries Vlorë figured in the conflicts between the Byzantine Empire and the Norman Kingdom of Sicily. A Venetian fleet attacked it in 1321, and from 1346 to 1417 it was the capital of the Principality of Valona, at first a vassal of the Serbian Empire. The Ottomans captured it in 1417; Albanian rebels freed it in 1432, but it returned to Ottoman rule and became a sanjak centre under the name Avlonya. Venice held it briefly from 1690 to 1691. A Jewish community, settled with Ottoman support from 1426 and enlarged by exiles from Spain after 1492, numbered some 2,600 people in the censuses of 1506 and 1520, and traded between Europe and Ottoman cities.

On 28 November 1912, during the First Balkan War, Ismail Qemali headed the Albanian Declaration of Independence at Vlorë, and the city became Albania's first capital. Italy occupied it in 1914 and again in 1939, and under Enver Hoxha's communist government after the Second World War the port was leased to the Soviet Union as a submarine base until the break of 1961.

Vlorë is the third most populous city of Albania and the seat of Vlorë County. It is a major seaport and commercial centre, and its Museum of Independence stands in the 19th-century building where the founders of Albania signed the declaration. The Castle of Kaninë and the archaeological sites of Amantia and Oricum lie in the municipality. The city belongs to the cultural region of Labëria, known for polyphonic music that UNESCO has recognised.
volga: The Volga is 3,531 kilometres long and drains about 1,360,000 square kilometres, almost entirely within Russia. It rises at Volgoverkhov'e in Tver Oblast, in the Valdai Hills north-west of Moscow, and runs east past Tver, Yaroslavl, Nizhny Novgorod and Kazan before turning south past Samara, Saratov and Volgograd. Below Astrakhan it spreads into a delta of as many as 500 channels and smaller rivers and enters the Caspian Sea, an enclosed body of water, so the river reaches no ocean. Its main tributaries are the Kama, the Oka, the Vetluga and the Sura. It freezes over most of its length for three months each year.

The Volga–Oka region has been occupied for at least 9,000 years. In antiquity the river marked the boundary between the Cimmerians and the Scythians, and later between the Scythians and the Massagetae. Names for it survive from several peoples: Scythian Rahā, Herodotus's Oaros, and Turkic Itil, which gave modern forms such as the Tatar İdel. In the first millennium Slavic, Finno-Ugric, Scandinavian, Baltic and Turkic peoples lived along it, and Alans settled the Middle Volga between the 6th and 8th centuries.

The river was a trade route linking Scandinavia and the Slavic lands with Volga Bulgaria, Khazaria, Persia and the Arab world. Volga Bulgaria flourished where the Kama joins the Volga, and Khazaria controlled the lower stretches. Cities such as Atil, Saqsin and Sarai were among the largest of the medieval world. The Mongols founded the Golden Horde on the lower river, and its successor khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan were conquered by the Russians in the 16th century.

Catherine the Great invited foreigners to settle the region in 1763, and Germans responded in the largest numbers. In 1941 the remaining Volga Germans, about 400,000, were deported and many were forced into labour camps. During the Second World War the Battle of Stalingrad was fought on the river's bend, where Volgograd now stands.

The Volga is widely regarded as the national river of Russia, and its place in Russian literature and folklore is shown in the name Mother Volga. Soviet-era dams formed some of the largest reservoirs in the world, and building them involved the forced resettlement of many people and the flooding of the town of Mologa and of several monasteries. Canals connect it to the Black Sea, the Azov, Baltic and White seas, and Moscow.
volgograd: Volgograd lies on the western bank of the Volga and covers 859.4 square kilometres. It is the administrative centre and largest city of Volgograd Oblast, divided into eight districts. The city stands at the east end of the Volga–Don Canal, opened in 1952 to link the two great rivers of southern Russia, and is a major railway junction. Its climate is a hot-summer continental one with cold winters and low rainfall spread through the year.

The fortress of Tsaritsyn, named after the Tsaritsa River, stood near the mouth of that river and soon became the nucleus of a trading settlement. At the start of the 17th century its garrison numbered 350 to 400 people, and in 1607 it rebelled for six months against the troops of Tsar Vasili Shuisky. The Streltsy stationed there were paid to defend the Volga trade route from the Cossacks, though some joined the Cossacks themselves. The railway link to Moscow in 1871 connected the isolated area to the rest of the empire, and by the 1890s the economy rested on grain, naphtha, fish and salt.

Tsaritsyn came under Bolshevik control in November 1917, fell briefly to the White Army in mid-1919 and returned to Bolshevik control in January 1920. On 10 April 1925 it was renamed Stalingrad in honour of Joseph Stalin, then General Secretary of the Communist Party, for his role in its defence. Under Soviet rule minorities were targeted: the only Jewish school in the area was closed in 1926, and the synagogue was closed in 1929 after a campaign begun in 1928. The Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, consecrated in 1918, was closed in 1929, used as a motor depot and demolished in 1932.

The Battle of Stalingrad, the largest and bloodiest battle of the Second World War, earned the city the title of Hero City. On 10 November 1961 Nikita Khrushchev's administration renamed it Volgograd, after the river, as part of de-Stalinization. The change was controversial because of the city's importance as a symbol of resistance, and proposals to restore the old name were floated in 1984 but not accepted.

Volgograd has a little over one million inhabitants and remains an industrial city, with shipbuilding, oil refining, steel and aluminium production and heavy machinery. The Mamayev Kurgan memorial complex, the hill where some of the most intense fighting took place, is dominated by The Motherland Calls, an 85-metre statue. The Panorama Museum preserves Gerhardt's Mill in its bombed-out state, and Pavlov's House, another surviving monument of the battle, stands nearby. The Alexander Nevsky Cathedral was rebuilt as a replica and consecrated in 2021.
voltaire: François-Marie Arouet, later known as Voltaire, was born in Paris, the youngest of five children of François Arouet, a lawyer and minor treasury official, and Marie Marguerite Daumard, whose family was of the lowest rank of the French nobility. He gave his birth date as 20 February 1694, claiming to be the illegitimate son of a nobleman, but his birth is dated to 21 November 1694, with a baptism on 22 November. The Jesuits educated him at the Collège Louis-le-Grand from 1704 to 1711, where he was taught Latin, theology and rhetoric.

Voltaire's play Artémire flopped in 1720, and he turned to an epic poem about Henry IV of France, La Henriade. Denied a licence to publish it, he went north in August 1722 to find a publisher outside France, and in the Netherlands he was impressed by the openness and tolerance of Dutch society. The poem was printed clandestinely in Rouen, and when copies were smuggled into Paris it was an instant success. His play Mariamne failed in 1724 but did better in a reworked version in April 1725.

In early 1726 Guy Auguste de Rohan-Chabot had Voltaire beaten by servants after a quarrel about his name change. When Voltaire challenged him to a duel, the powerful Rohan family had him imprisoned without trial in the Bastille on 17 April 1726. Fearing indefinite imprisonment, he asked to be exiled to England instead, and on 2 May he was escorted from the Bastille to Calais and embarked.

He was one of the first authors to be commercially successful internationally, and wrote more than 20,000 letters and 2,000 books and pamphlets. In February 1778 he returned to Paris for the first time in over 25 years, partly for the opening of his tragedy Irène, and died there on 30 May 1778. The Church had refused him a Christian burial because he would not retract his criticism, so friends buried him secretly at the Abbey of Scellières.

Voltaire produced plays, poems, novels, essays, histories and scientific expositions. His best-known work is the novella Candide (1759), which ridicules Gottfried Leibniz's belief that this is the best of all possible worlds. His History of Charles XII (1731), The Age of Louis XIV (1751) and Essay on the Customs and the Spirit of the Nations (1756) set aside diplomatic and military narrative for customs, social history and the arts and sciences, and treated Europe as a whole.
